title: China flies a stealth drone off a catapult amphibious ship as Britain sets a 3% GDP defence target
subhead: The PLAN confirmed the GJ-21's first launch and arrested recovery aboard the Type 076 Sichuan, while London laid out 3% by 2030 and a $2.1bn Patriot package for Kyiv was approved under allied funding.

sections.heading: China confirms the GJ-21's first carrier-style recovery aboard the Sichuan
sections.body:
The People's Liberation Army Navy confirmed that the GJ-21, its first shipborne stealth reconnaissance and strike drone, completed a first launch and arrested landing aboard the Sichuan, the lead ship of the Type 076 amphibious assault ship class, per Xinhua reporting carried by Aviacionline. The announcement carried notable caveats: no images or video were released, and neither the date, location nor number of launch-recovery cycles was disclosed.

Why the ship matters more than the aircraft: the Sichuan displaces more than 40,000 tons, was launched on 27 December 2024, and pairs an integrated electric power system with electromagnetic catapults, arresting gear and automatic landing guidance. The GJ-21 is a turbojet-powered flying-wing derivative of the GJ-11 that, per Chinese specialists quoted by the Global Times, exceeds ten tons at takeoff weight — too heavy for conventional deck launch, which is exactly why the EMALS installation is the enabler. As Aviacionline notes, this makes the Sichuan effectively the first catapult-equipped ship designed around combat drones rather than a supplement to the carrier Fujian.

The capability is not yet operational. Official commissioning of the Sichuan, compatibility testing with other unmanned types, and integration with the Fujian's escort group remain pending.
sections.whyItMatters: A catapult-capable drone deck expands what a 40,000-ton ship can do without a full carrier air wing — a cheaper route to fixed-wing reach than building more carriers. The absence of imagery means the claim itself is a signal about confidence, not proof of a mature capability.

sections.heading: Britain puts a number on it: 3% of GDP by 2030, 3.5% by 2035
sections.body:
John Healey set out on 28 October an intention to raise UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, rising to 3.5% by 2035 conditional on the first target being met, Defence Industry Europe reported. The commitment is meant to fund the recently announced Defence Investment Plan.

The funding is the weak point. Sources have not been identified; a public spending review next year is expected to determine how the increases are paid for. Alongside the target, Whitehall announced a task force on innovative defence financing to pull in private and foreign capital, with the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank expected to provide up to £5 billion over four years. Deeper joint procurement is planned with the Netherlands, Poland and Finland, a new MoD regulatory team will work on making uncrewed-systems testing easier, and the government signalled an intention to provide £10 billion in assistance to Ukraine without a delivery timetable.

Separately, negotiations continue over financing R&D for a dual-use gas turbine Rolls-Royce could design, estimated at £2.5 billion over a decade.
sections.whyItMatters: A headline percentage without an identified funding source is a planning assumption, not a budget. The industrial measures — joint procurement with the Netherlands, Poland and Finland, and uncrewed testing deregulation — are the parts with near-term effect.

sections.heading: Washington clears 500 Patriot interceptors for Ukraine, paid for by allies
sections.body:
The US State Department approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, Reuters reported via the Jerusalem Post — one of the most significant defensive arms steps of the second Trump administration.

The payment structure is the story. Kyiv will fund the buy through contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed via a programme called US JUMPSTART, plus national funds financed by the EU's Ukraine Support Loan. JUMPSTART pools allied donations to purchase weapons, services and training for Ukraine. The channel was previously used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million from Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor.

Delivery will not be quick; the report notes weapons sales typically take years, though Ukraine's air-defence emergency may accelerate the timeline. The approval came after Zelensky said Kyiv had waited almost a month for the US to sign off on interceptors, and against a backdrop of continued mass strikes — a Russian drone attack on a Dnipro rail platform killed at least 14 people on Thursday.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe now pays for American interceptors to defend Ukraine. That model keeps US production lines in the loop while transferring the fiscal burden — useful for Washington, but it hardens Ukraine's dependence on a supply chain it does not control.

sections.heading: Raytheon's munitions output up more than 90% as four multiyear contracts land
sections.body:
RTX chairman and CEO Chris Calio told investors on the 20 October earnings call that Raytheon's output across critical munitions is up more than 90% year-over-year in the first nine months of 2026, with material receipts up double digits. Management did not disclose which programmes or quantities were included, per Defence Industry Europe.

The next wave is contractual. Four multiyear agreements covering Tomahawk, AMRAAM, SM-6 and SM-3 IB are worth roughly $70 billion combined and support rate increases of two to four times current levels, with full-rate production targeted for 2030. Raytheon added 150 new suppliers in 2025 alone and is working with the Pentagon on streamlined testing, obsolescence and new supply qualification.

Bottlenecks remain real: rocket motors are the named constraint, RTX is spreading risk across motor manufacturers rather than acquiring one, and Calio acknowledged competition with the AI sector for certain inputs and materials. Critical minerals are being secured via government-backed long-term commitments through 2027 and beyond. Raytheon sales rose 14% to $8 billion in Q3, and the business closed the quarter with a $130 billion backlog after $52.3 billion in orders.
sections.whyItMatters: The 90% figure measures recovery from a low base with unspecified contents; the $70 billion in multiyear contracts is the harder number. The binding constraint is now rocket motors and minerals, not factory floor space.

sections.heading: North Korea tests cluster warheads for tactical ballistic missiles
sections.body:
North Korea test-fired cluster-bomb warheads on 31 October, KCNA reported, in what state media described as an assessment of a warhead 'to be tipped on tactical ballistic missiles'. Officials claimed the weapon can devastate a target area of 12 to 13 hectares at highest-density power — AFP, via Malay Mail, noted the claim is unverified.

The Missile Administration's director said units would be enabled 'within this year' to select and use these types according to operational aims. Kim Jong Un did not attend, unlike the April cluster-warhead test he oversaw with his daughter Ju Ae. The test followed recent trials of attack drones, a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, and came amid heightened tension over a border landmine blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers — which Pyongyang denies.
sections.whyItMatters: Area-effect warheads on short-range ballistic missiles are a cheaper way to threaten Seoul-area rear areas and airbases than precision munitions. That Pyongyang is standardising training across a widening family of systems points to a maturing force, not just a test programme.

sections.heading: DIA: Russia's nuclear-armed satellite could disable thousands of spacecraft
sections.body:
The US Defense Intelligence Agency said Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon that could disable thousands of spacecraft and disrupt global services, per Defence Industry Europe. The assessment states Russia is pursuing the system 'despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty', which bars placing nuclear weapons or other WMD in Earth orbit.

The DIA flagged Cosmos 2553, launched in February 2022 into an unusual isolated orbit, and warned that radiation belts from a detonation could persist for years, damaging satellites that survive the initial pulse. The agency framed the programme within a broader Russian push against US space advantages — from jamming and sensor blinding to destruction of spacecraft and ground infrastructure — and quoted the pre-invasion 2022 Viasat malware operation that disrupted services for 50,000 users across Ukraine and Europe. Russia's ground-based lasers and the Peresvet system, deployed with five strategic missile divisions, were also cited.
sections.whyItMatters: The threat is not military-only. Commercial navigation, weather and communications constellations are in the blast radius, which makes this a deterrence problem for civilian infrastructure and a live argument for space-domain budgeting.

sections.heading: Iraq rebuilds air defence from four suppliers at once
sections.body:
Baghdad is assembling an air-defence network from multiple foreign sources simultaneously. Armed forces spokesperson Sabah al-Numan said in an October 16 interview with Rudaw that Iraq has 'contracted with the United States of America, Turkey, and South Korea' and expects a first system within months, as reported via Yahoo/The New Region.

The gap is acute: remaining US troops in Iraqi Kurdistan withdrew by September under the 2024 phased withdrawal agreement, taking with them air defences including a Patriot battery that had shielded Erbil during this year's Iran war. Iraq's defence ministry has said a directive exists to extend air defence to Iraqi Kurdistan within three to six years. Earlier signals included Turkish approval to supply air-defence systems (per parliament defence committee member Mahmoud al-Shammari), a similar agreement with France during PM Ali al-Zaidi's September visit, and a letter of intent between Harmattan AI and Iraq's defence ministry on autonomous air-defence systems.
sections.whyItMatters: Four suppliers means four logistics chains, four training pipelines and no single integration authority — the classic condition for a system that looks networked on paper and does not talk in practice. It also puts Turkish and South Korean exporters into a market Washington once dominated.

bottomLine: China's GJ-21 recovery aboard the Sichuan is the day's most consequential defence development: a catapult-equipped drone ship at 40,000 tons offers fixed-wing reach at a fraction of carrier cost, even if Beijing released no imagery and the capability is years from operational. Britain's 3% by 2030 target is directionally important but unfunded pending next year's spending review, while the $2.1 billion Patriot package for Ukraine shows Europe paying Raytheon and Lockheed Martin to arm Kyiv. Behind these, RTX's 90% munitions output gain and $70 billion in multiyear missile contracts confirm that Western stockpile rebuilding is now a decade-long industrial programme constrained by rocket motors and critical minerals, not demand.
sources: Aviacionline, Xinhua, Global Times, Defence Industry Europe, Reuters (via Jerusalem Post), AeroTime, KCNA/AFP (via Malay Mail), US Defense Intelligence Agency, Rudaw, The New Region, Yahoo News
